mainEntity.name: What are access modifiers in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Access modifiers in Java are keywords that control the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, variables, and constructors. Java provides four access modifiers: public (accessible from everywhere), protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses), default/package-private (accessible only within the same package — no keyword used), and private (accessible only within the same class). They are the foundation of encapsulation — one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between private, protected, and public in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: private: accessible only within the declaring class — tightest restriction. protected: accessible within the same package AND in subclasses (even in different packages) — enables controlled inheritance. public: accessible from anywhere — widest visibility. default (no keyword): accessible only within the same package. The rule of thumb: use the most restrictive modifier that still allows your code to function. Prefer private for fields, public for API methods, and protected only when subclassing requires it.

mainEntity.name: Can a class be private in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A top-level class (declared directly in a .java file) can only be public or default (package-private). It CANNOT be private or protected — this causes a compile-time error. However, inner classes (nested classes declared inside another class) CAN be private, protected, public, or default. A private inner class is accessible only within the enclosing class. This is commonly used for helper classes or implementation details hidden from external code.

mainEntity.name: What is default access modifier in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The default access modifier (also called package-private) is applied when NO modifier keyword is specified. A member with default access is accessible to all classes within the same package but is invisible to classes in other packages — even subclasses in a different package cannot access it. It is the middle ground between private (class-only) and protected (package + subclasses). It is commonly used for classes and methods that are internal implementation details of a package and not meant to be part of the public API.

mainEntity.name: Can we override a private method in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Private methods cannot be overridden in Java. Since private methods are not visible to subclasses, they cannot participate in Java's dynamic dispatch (runtime polymorphism). If a subclass defines a method with the same signature as a parent's private method, it is simply a NEW method in the subclass — not an override. The @Override annotation on such a method causes a compile-time error, confirming that no actual overriding occurred. This is method hiding, not overriding.

sections.title: What are Access Modifiers in Java?

blocks.text: Access modifiers (also called access specifiers) in Java are keywords that define the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, constructors, and fields. They are the primary mechanism Java provides to implement encapsulation — the OOP principle of hiding internal implementation details and exposing only what is necessary.

Java provides four access modifiers: public, private, protected, and default (package-private — applied when no modifier keyword is written). Each defines a different level of visibility, ranging from completely open (public) to completely restricted (private).

In real-world applications, access control is everywhere: a BankAccount class keeps its balance field private so only its own methods can modify it. A paymentGateway method is public so external systems can call it. An internal helper method like validateCVV() is private so no outside class can bypass security. This careful control is what separates robust production code from fragile code that anyone can break.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Access Modifiers at a Glance
blocks.text: Java has 4 access levels: (1) public — visible everywhere: same class, same package, subclass, other package. (2) protected — visible in same class, same package, and subclasses (even in different packages). (3) default (no keyword) — visible only in same class and same package; NOT visible in other packages, even subclasses. (4) private — visible only in the same class; not even subclasses can access it. Rule of thumb: always use the MOST RESTRICTIVE modifier that still allows your code to function.

The public modifier grants unrestricted access from anywhere in the program — the same class, the same package, subclasses in different packages, and completely unrelated classes in other packages. It is the most permissive modifier. public is used for class definitions that form the API — the intentional public contract that other code is meant to use.

items.title: Where public Can Be Applied
items.text:
• Top-level classes (the class itself)
• Methods (instance and static)
• Fields/variables (though usually combined with final for constants)
• Constructors
• Interfaces and their members
• Enum declarations
• Nested/inner classes

items.title: Visibility Scope
items.text:
Accessible from:
✅ Same class
✅ Same package
✅ Subclass in same package
✅ Subclass in different package
✅ Non-subclass in different package
→ No restrictions — visible from everywhere in the program.

items.title: One public Class Per File Rule
items.text: A .java file can contain ONLY ONE public top-level class, and the filename MUST match that class name exactly (case-sensitive). Example: PublicDemo.java must contain 'public class PublicDemo'. Violating this is a compile-time error. A file can have multiple non-public (default) classes, but only one public class.

blocks.label: PublicModifierDemo.java
lines: // public field — accessible from anywhere (avoid for mutable state)
public static final double TAX_RATE = 0.18; // ✅ OK — constant
// public mutable field — BAD PRACTICE (exposed to modification)
public String name; // ❌ Avoid — use private + getter/setter
// public method — part of the API contract
// ✅ Can access public class from different package

blocks.title: ⚠️ public Fields Are Almost Always a Mistake
blocks.text: Making instance fields public exposes your class's internal state to direct modification by ANY code. Once public, you cannot add validation, logging, or change internal representation without breaking all callers. Always make fields private and expose them through controlled public getters/setters. The only accepted exception: public static final constants (e.g., Math.PI, Integer.MAX_VALUE).

The private modifier is the most restrictive access level. A private member is accessible only within the class where it is declared — not from subclasses, not from other classes in the same package, not from anywhere else. private is the correct default for all class fields and implementation-detail methods, forming the foundation of encapsulation.

items.title: Where private Can Be Applied
items.text:
• Fields/variables (most common use)
• Methods (helper/utility methods)
• Constructors (Singleton pattern, factory pattern)
• Nested/inner classes
• ❌ Cannot be applied to top-level classes

items.title: Visibility Scope
items.text:
Accessible from:
✅ Same class only
❌ Same package (other classes)
❌ Subclass in same package
❌ Subclass in different package
❌ Other packages
→ Total isolation within the declaring class.

items.title: Why private is the Right Default
items.text: Start everything as private. Only promote visibility (to protected or public) when external access is genuinely required. This is the 'Principle of Least Privilege' — give the minimum access needed. It enables: safe refactoring (internals can change freely), validation before state changes (via setters), immutability (no setter = immutable field), and better encapsulation.

blocks.label: BankAccount.java — private in Action
lines: // ✅ private fields — no outside code can directly modify balance
// ✅ public constructor — outsiders can create accounts
public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName, double initialDeposit) {
// Validation in constructor — impossible with public fields
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Initial deposit cannot be negative");
// ✅ public API methods — controlled access to private state
if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit must be positive");
if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
return balance; // Read-only access — no setter for balance
// ✅ private helper methods — implementation details hidden
if (frozen) throw new IllegalStateException("Account is frozen");
private void logTransaction(String type, double amount) {

blocks.title: 💡 private Constructor — Singleton & Utility Class Pattern
blocks.text: Making a constructor private prevents external instantiation. This is deliberately used in two patterns: (1) Singleton: 'private static final BankConfig INSTANCE = new BankConfig();' with 'public static BankConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }' — only one object ever exists. (2) Utility class: 'private MathUtils() {}' on a class with only static methods — prevents pointless instantiation of a class that has no instance state (like java.lang.Math).

The protected modifier grants access to the same class, same package, AND all subclasses — even subclasses in different packages. It sits between default (package-only) and public (everywhere). protected is designed specifically for inheritance scenarios — when a parent class wants to share implementation details with its children without exposing them to the entire world.

items.title: Where protected Can Be Applied
items.text:
• Methods (intended for subclass use or override)
• Fields (shared internal state with subclasses)
• Constructors (force subclassing — e.g., abstract base class)
• Nested/inner classes
• ❌ Cannot be applied to top-level classes

items.title: Visibility Scope
items.text:
Accessible from:
✅ Same class
✅ Same package (all classes)
✅ Subclass in same package
✅ Subclass in different package
❌ Non-subclass in different package
→ Key: package OR subclass, but NOT arbitrary outside classes.

items.title: protected vs default — Key Difference
items.text: Both allow same-package access. The difference: protected ALSO allows subclass access across packages. default does NOT. If you have a class in package 'com.app.base' with a default method, and a subclass in 'com.app.ui', the subclass CANNOT access that method. Make it protected to enable cross-package inheritance while still blocking arbitrary external code.

blocks.label: ProtectedModifierDemo.java
lines: // protected field — subclasses can access and set this
// protected constructor — forces use of subclasses
// public abstract method — subclasses MUST implement
// protected method — shared logic for subclasses, hidden from outside
// protected utility for rendering — subclasses may override or call
super(color, 1.0); // ✅ Can call protected parent constructor
// ✅ Can access protected parent method from subclass (different package)
drawBorder(); // ✅ Can call protected parent method
// In a completely unrelated class (different package, NOT a subclass):
// s.drawBorder();       // ❌ Compile error — protected, not a subclass

blocks.title: ⚠️ Tricky: protected Access Through Inheritance Is Limited
blocks.text: A subclass can access a parent's protected member through its OWN reference or 'super', but NOT through a reference of the parent type from a different package. Example: in class Child extends Parent (different package), 'this.protectedField' is ✅ OK. But 'Parent p = new Parent(); p.protectedField' is ❌ COMPILE ERROR — even inside the Child class. This is one of the most commonly misunderstood rules of Java access control.

The default access modifier — also called package-private — is applied when no access modifier keyword is written. A member with default access is visible to all classes within the same package but is completely hidden from classes in other packages, including subclasses in different packages. It is the "internal to this package" visibility level.

items.title: How to Apply Default Access
items.text:
Simply write NOTHING — no keyword at all:
• class DatabaseHelper { }  // default class
• void executeQuery() { }   // default method
• int rowCount;              // default field
Do NOT write 'default' as a keyword for access — 'default' is only a keyword in switch and interface default methods, not as an access modifier.

items.title: Visibility Scope
items.text:
Accessible from:
✅ Same class
✅ Same package (all classes)
❌ Subclass in different package
❌ Non-subclass in different package
→ Package boundary is the visibility limit.

items.title: When to Use Default Access
items.text: Use default access for: (1) Implementation classes not meant to be in the public API — e.g., a Helper or Impl class. (2) Package-internal utilities shared among classes in the same module/package. (3) Classes intentionally restricted to a bounded context (Domain-Driven Design bounded contexts). Well-designed Java packages often have 1-2 public API classes and several default (internal) classes.

blocks.label: DefaultAccessDemo.java
lines: // Not accessible from other packages — intentional
// Default method — only classes in same package can call this
private PaymentValidator validator = new PaymentValidator(); // ✅ Same package
public boolean processPayment(double amount, String currency) {
PaymentProcessor proc = new PaymentProcessor(); // ✅ public class
// PaymentValidator v = new PaymentValidator();   // ❌ Compile error

sections.title: Access Modifier Comparison Table — At a Glance

blocks.text: This table summarises the complete visibility matrix for all four Java access modifiers across every possible access location.

blocks.title: 💡 Memory Trick — Widening Visibility Order
blocks.text: Remember the order from most restrictive to least restrictive: private → default → protected → public. Think of it as expanding circles: private = within the class wall. default = within the package fence. protected = package fence + inheritance bridge. public = no walls at all. Each level includes all access of the level before it, plus adds more.

sections.title: Class-Level vs Member-Level Access — Two Distinct Contexts

blocks.text: Access modifiers work at two distinct levels in Java: the class level (controlling access to the class itself) and the member level (controlling access to fields, methods, and constructors inside the class). The rules are different at each level, and confusing them is a common source of errors.

items.title: Class-Level Access (Top-Level Classes)
items.text: Top-level classes can only be public or default (package-private). They CANNOT be private or protected — this is a compile-time error. A public class is accessible from any package. A default class is only accessible from within its own package. One .java file = maximum one public class (must match filename).

items.title: Member-Level Access (Fields, Methods, Constructors)
items.text: Members of a class can use all four modifiers: private, default, protected, and public. Member-level access is determined first by the class-level access. Even if a method is public, if the class itself is default (package-private), outside packages cannot reach that method — the class is not even visible to them.

items.title: Nested Class Access
items.text: Inner classes (nested inside another class) can use all four modifiers. A private inner class is accessible only within the enclosing class. A public inner class is accessible anywhere (though the outer class must also be reachable). Static nested classes follow the same rules as regular classes.

blocks.label: ClassVsMemberAccess.java
lines: // ✅ public top-level class — accessible from other packages
// Member-level modifiers — all four are valid here
private   int orderId;          // Only Order class
double    totalAmount;          // Default — same package only
public    String orderStatus;   // Everywhere (but bad practice for mutable field)
// private constructor — prevents direct instantiation (factory pattern)
// public factory method — the intended way to create orders
if (orderId <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid order ID");
// ✅ private nested class — only Order can use this
// ✅ default nested class — accessible in same package
// ❌ private class MyClass { }   // Compile error — top-level class cannot be private
// ❌ protected class MyClass { } // Compile error — top-level class cannot be protected

sections.title: Access Modifiers with Inheritance — Overriding Rules

blocks.text: Access modifiers interact with inheritance in specific, important ways. When a subclass overrides a parent method, Java enforces a critical rule: the overriding method cannot reduce visibility — it can only maintain or widen the access level. This ensures that code relying on the parent's interface continues to work with any subclass (Liskov Substitution Principle).

items.title: Widening Access — Allowed
items.text:
An overriding method CAN increase visibility:
• protected → public ✅
• default → protected ✅
• default → public ✅
• private → (cannot override, so not applicable)
Widening is always safe — if callers could call the parent version, they can certainly call a more accessible version.

items.title: Narrowing Access — Compile Error
items.text:
An overriding method CANNOT reduce visibility:
• public → protected ❌ Compile error
• public → default ❌ Compile error
• public → private ❌ Compile error
• protected → default ❌ Compile error
Narrowing would break code that expects the parent's public interface to work on any subclass.

items.title: private Methods — Cannot Be Overridden
items.text: Private methods are not visible to subclasses, so they CANNOT be overridden. If a subclass declares a method with the same name and signature as a parent's private method, it is a completely NEW method — not an override. Using @Override annotation on it causes a compile error. This is called method hiding (for static methods) or simply a new unrelated method (for instance methods).

blocks.label: AccessWithInheritance.java
lines: private String vin;          // Not inherited — completely private
protected String fuelType;   // Accessible in subclasses
// ✅ MAINTAINING access: public → public (same level, always allowed)
// protected String getInfo() { } // ERROR — cannot reduce from public to protected
// This is a NEW method, NOT an override of private performInternalDiagnostic()
System.out.println("EV diagnostic — battery, motor, regenerative braking");
// Cannot call: super.performInternalDiagnostic(); // ❌ private — not visible

sections.title: Encapsulation — The Core Purpose of Access Modifiers

blocks.text: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming (alongside Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction). It means bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class), while restricting direct access to the data. Access modifiers are the mechanism that makes encapsulation possible in Java.

items.title: Data Hiding
items.text: Make all fields private. External code cannot directly read or modify internal state. Every access goes through controlled methods. Benefit: the class can enforce invariants — guarantees about its own state that should always hold (e.g., age can never be negative, balance can never go below minimumBalance).

items.title: Controlled Access via Getters/Setters
items.text: Provide public getters (read access) and optionally public setters (write access) for fields that need external visibility. Setters can validate input before modifying state. Read-only fields have a getter but no setter. Write-only fields (rare) have a setter but no getter. This gives you full control over every read and write.

items.title: Freedom to Change Internals
items.text: Once fields are private, you can change their internal representation at any time without breaking callers. Example: storing a phone number as String internally but exposing it as a formatted PhoneNumber object through the getter. Or switching from ArrayList to LinkedList for an internal collection. Callers never know — they only use the public API.

blocks.label: EncapsulatedEmployee.java
lines: // ✅ ALL fields private — enforces controlled access
private final int    employeeId;   // Immutable — no setter
public Employee(int employeeId, String name, String department,
if (salary < 0)        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Salary cannot be negative");
if (age < 18 || age > 65) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age out of range");
if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
// Read-only getter (no setter — ID is final/immutable)
// Standard getter and setter with validation
if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
if (salary < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Salary cannot be negative");
if (age < 18 || age > 65) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age out of range");
// Business method — uses private state without exposing it

sections.title: Access Modifiers in Interfaces — Special Rules

blocks.text: Interfaces in Java have special access modifier rules that differ from classes. Understanding these is essential for writing correct Java interfaces, especially since Java 8, 9, and later versions added default, static, and private methods to interfaces.

items.title: Interface Methods
items.text:
• Abstract methods: implicitly public — no other modifier allowed (private/protected/default cause compile error in abstract context).
• default methods (Java 8+): must be public (explicitly or implicitly).
• static methods (Java 8+): must be public (default) or private (Java 9+).
• private methods (Java 9+): allowed — used as internal helpers for default/static methods. NOT inherited by implementing classes.

items.title: Interface Fields
items.text: All fields in an interface are implicitly: public, static, and final — i.e., they are constants. You cannot make interface fields private or protected. Writing 'int MAX = 100;' in an interface is automatically 'public static final int MAX = 100;'. Attempting to assign them in implementing classes is a compile error.

items.title: Interface Itself
items.text: A top-level interface can only be public or default (package-private) — same as classes. A public interface is accessible everywhere. A default interface is package-private. Nested interfaces inside a class can be public, protected, default, or private. When implementing an interface method, the implementing class method MUST be public — it cannot reduce visibility.

blocks.label: InterfaceAccessModifiers.java
lines: // Implicitly: public abstract — no modifier needed
default String formatAmount(double amount, String currency) {
// ✅ private method (Java 9+) — helper for default methods
// Implementing class MUST use public for all interface methods
public boolean processPayment(double amount, String currency) { // ✅ Must be public
// ❌ Cannot do this — would narrow interface's public to protected

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Errors That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These mistakes appear consistently in Java beginner and intermediate code. Each one either causes a compile-time error or — worse — silently violates the encapsulation principle, creating fragile code that breaks during maintenance.

blocks.label: AccessModifierMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: public mutable fields — breaks encapsulation
public double price;  // ❌ Anyone can set: product.price = -999;
public int stock;     // ❌ No validation possible
// ✅ Fix: private fields with validated setters
if (price < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Price cannot be negative");
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Making a class private at top level
// private class Config { }  // Compile error — top-level class cannot be private
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Narrowing access in subclass override
// protected void speak() { }  // ❌ Compile error — narrows public to protected
public void speak() { System.out.println("Woof!"); } // ✅ Same or wider
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Expecting protected to mean 'subclass only'
// (In same package, ALL classes — not just subclasses — can access protected members)
System.out.println(p.secret); // ✅ Works! Same package, not just subclasses
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Overriding private method (it is not an override)
public void run() { helper(); } // Calls Base's private helper
// This is a NEW method — NOT an override
// run() in Base still calls Base's private helper — polymorphism does NOT apply
// new Derived().run() → prints 'Base helper', NOT 'Derived helper'
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Forgetting that interface methods implementing must be public
// void fly() { }          // ❌ Reduces public to default — compile error
public void fly() { }      // ✅ Must explicitly be public

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These access modifier anti-patterns are among the top reasons for failed code reviews in professional Java teams. Each one violates fundamental OOP principles and creates long-term maintenance problems.

items.title: God Class with All-Public Fields
items.text: A class where all fields are public is not encapsulation — it is a glorified struct. Any class can modify its state directly, making it impossible to enforce invariants, add validation, or refactor internals. Every field should start private. Only promote visibility when genuinely needed, and almost never to public for mutable fields.

items.title: Anemic Domain Model
items.text: A class with all-private fields but only getters and setters, with no business logic — just data containers. This is anti-OOP. Business logic that works with the data belongs IN the class, not scattered in service classes. An Employee should have calculateBonus(), not just getSalary()/setSalary(). Tell, don't ask.

items.title: Using protected Instead of private by Default
items.text: Making all fields protected 'in case subclasses need them' is lazy access control. protected exposes internals to the entire package AND all future subclasses. This tightly couples parent and child classes, making the parent hard to refactor. Keep fields private; provide protected methods if subclasses need specific behaviour — not raw field access.

items.title: Unnecessary Public API — Leaking Internals
items.text: Making internal helper methods public because 'it might be useful later' pollutes the public API. Once public, removing or renaming a method is a breaking change. Every public method is a contract you must maintain forever. Use private or package-private for implementation details. Add to public API only with deliberate intent.

items.title: Breaking Encapsulation via Returning Mutable References
items.text: Returning a reference to a private mutable collection or array defeats encapsulation even with a private field: 'public List<Order> getOrders() { return orders; }' — the caller now holds a direct reference to the internal list and can modify it. Return a defensive copy: 'return Collections.unmodifiableList(orders)' or 'return new ArrayList<>(orders)'.

items.title: Reflection to Access Private Members
items.text: Using Java Reflection to access private fields (field.setAccessible(true)) in production code is an extreme violation of encapsulation — it bypasses all access control. It makes code brittle (breaks when field names change), causes security issues in modular Java (Java 9+ module system blocks this), and signals a design flaw. If external code needs access, provide a proper API.

blocks.label: AccessAntiPatterns.java
lines: return items;  // ❌ Caller gets direct reference — can modify!
// cart.getItems().clear(); // ❌ Clears internal list — bypasses all control!
// ✅ FIX: Return defensive copy or unmodifiable view
// Option 1: Unmodifiable view — throws on mutation attempt
// Option 2: Defensive copy — independent copy, mutations don't affect internal state
// ✅ BEST: Provide specific methods instead of exposing the collection
if (item == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Item cannot be null");
// field.setAccessible(true); // ❌ Breaks encapsulation, brittle, security risk
// → If you need this in production code, the design has a problem — fix the API.

blocks.text: The following examples show access modifier usage patterns found in real enterprise Java codebases — Spring Boot application layers with deliberate, idiomatic access control at each level.

// private — internal collection never exposed directly
private final List<String> roles = new ArrayList<>();
// package-private constructor — only factory/builder in same package creates instances
UserAccount(String userId, String email, String displayName) {
// public read-only accessors for immutable fields
// public controlled mutators with business logic
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Display name cannot be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Display name too long");
// Business state — read publicly, changed only through business methods
// Business methods — encapsulate state transitions with rules
// ✅ Unmodifiable view — callers read roles, cannot modify internal list

blocks.label: AbstractRepository.java — protected Template Method Pattern
lines: // Abstract base — default (package-private) access — internal framework class
// protected — subclasses must access this to perform DB operations
// public API — these are the operations callers use
// protected template methods — shared infrastructure, overridable behaviour
// Default: no-op. Subclasses can override to add audit timestamps.
// Default: no-op. Subclasses can override to publish domain events.
// private — internal framework utility, hidden even from subclasses
// public concrete class — this is what application code sees
public class UserRepository extends AbstractRepository<UserAccount, String> {
// ✅ Uses protected connection field from parent
return connection.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", userId);
// ✅ Overrides protected template — adds audit timestamp
public List<UserAccount> findAll()              { /* implementation */ return null; }
public UserAccount save(UserAccount entity)     { /* implementation */ return null; }

sections.title: Java Access Modifier Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, campus placements, and OCPJP/OCA certification exams.

items.q: Q1. What are the four access modifiers in Java and what is their order of visibility?
items.a: Java has four access modifiers in order from most restrictive to least restrictive: (1) private — accessible only within the declaring class. (2) default (no keyword) — accessible within the same package. (3) protected — accessible within the same package AND in subclasses across packages. (4) public — accessible from everywhere. Memory aid: private < default < protected < public. Each level is a superset of the previous: public includes everything protected does, which includes everything default does.

items.q: Q2. Can we declare a top-level class as private or protected in Java?
items.a: No. Top-level classes (declared directly in a .java file, not inside another class) can ONLY be public or default (package-private). Declaring a top-level class as private or protected is a compile-time error. The reason: private would mean only the same class can access it — which is meaningless for a top-level class. protected would mean package + subclasses — but subclassing requires the class to be visible first, creating a circular dependency. Inner classes (nested inside another class), however, CAN use all four modifiers.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between protected and default (package-private) access?
items.a: Both allow access from the same package. The critical difference: protected ALSO allows access from subclasses in DIFFERENT packages, while default does NOT. Example: class Parent with a default method in 'com.app.base'. A subclass in 'com.app.ui' CANNOT access that method. Make it protected and the subclass CAN access it. So: default = package boundary only. protected = package boundary + inheritance bridge across packages. Use protected deliberately for template methods, shared internal state, or constructors of abstract base classes.

items.q: Q4. Can a subclass reduce the visibility of an overridden method?
items.a: No — this is a compile-time error. Java's override rules require that the overriding method's access level be the SAME or WIDER than the parent's. This enforces the Liskov Substitution Principle: if code works with a Parent reference, it must work equally well with any subclass reference. Narrowing visibility would break this guarantee. Allowed widening: protected → public ✅. Same level: public → public ✅. Narrowing: public → protected ❌ (compile error). The only exception: private methods cannot be overridden at all — they are not inherited.

items.q: Q5. Can we override a private method in Java?
items.a: No. Private methods are not visible to subclasses — they are completely hidden within the declaring class. Therefore they cannot participate in Java's method overriding (dynamic dispatch). If a subclass declares a method with the same name and signature as a parent's private method, Java treats it as a BRAND NEW method in the subclass — not an override. Adding @Override annotation to such a method causes a compile error confirming no override occurred. This is an important distinction: private methods are fully excluded from the inheritance mechanism.

items.q: Q6. What is the default access modifier in Java? How is it different from 'default' in switch or interface?
items.a: The default access modifier is package-private visibility — applied when NO modifier keyword is written. It has no keyword — writing 'default' as an access modifier is a compile error. Confusingly, Java uses the word 'default' in two other contexts: (1) switch statement default case: 'default: ...' — completely unrelated. (2) Interface default methods (Java 8+): 'default void method() {}' — provides a default implementation, must be public. These three uses of 'default' are entirely different language features that happen to share a keyword. For access control, silence = package-private.

items.q: Q7. What access modifiers are allowed for interface methods in Java?
items.a: Interface method access depends on the method type: Abstract methods (traditional): implicitly public — no explicit modifier allowed. Writing protected/private/default causes a compile error. Default methods (Java 8+): implicitly public — must be public. Static methods (Java 8+): implicitly public, but can be private (Java 9+). Private methods (Java 9+): must be explicitly private — used as internal helpers for default/static methods. NOT inherited by implementing classes. When a class implements an interface method, that implementation MUST be public — it cannot reduce the interface's implicit public contract.

items.q: Q8. What happens when a package-private class has a public method?
items.a: The public method is only reachable by code that can first reach the class. If the class itself is package-private (default), then code in other packages cannot see the class at all — so even though the method is technically public, outside-package code cannot call it. The class acts as a visibility ceiling. This is intentional design: you can have a package-internal class with public methods (so same-package code calls them cleanly) while preventing those methods from being part of the external API.

items.q: Q9. What is encapsulation and how do access modifiers support it?
items.a: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a class, while restricting direct external access to the internal data. Access modifiers enforce encapsulation: private fields ensure external code cannot directly read or modify internal state. Public methods provide a controlled interface — with validation, logging, and business logic — for all access. This gives three key benefits: (1) Invariant enforcement — invalid states are impossible because all modifications go through controlled setters. (2) Refactoring freedom — internal representation can change without breaking callers. (3) API stability — public interface is stable while implementation evolves.

items.q: Q10. In a protected field in a parent class, can a subclass in a different package access it using a parent reference?
items.a: No — this is one of the most commonly misunderstood Java rules. A subclass in a different package can access a protected member through its OWN reference (this.protectedField or just protectedField) or through super. But it CANNOT access the protected member through a variable of the parent type. Example: inside class Child extends Parent (different package), 'this.protectedField' is ✅ valid, but 'Parent p = new Parent(); p.protectedField' is ❌ a compile error — even inside Child. This prevents unrelated objects of the parent type from being accessible through a subclass's inheritance privilege.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Access Modifier Knowledge

blocks.text: Attempt each question independently before reading the answer — active recall significantly improves retention.

items.a: Two issues: (1) 'radius' is public and mutable — anyone can set 'circle.radius = -5' or 'circle.radius = 100' without recalculating area, leaving the object in an inconsistent state. (2) 'area' should be computed, not stored as a public field — it must stay in sync with radius, which is impossible when both are public. Fix: make both fields private, provide 'getRadius()' and a 'setRadius(double r)' that also recalculates area, or better — make radius final (set once via constructor) and calculate area on demand via 'getArea() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }'. Immutable radius = no sync problem.

Compile error IF Config is a top-level class (declared directly in a .java file). Top-level classes can only be public or default — not private. The error is: 'modifier private not allowed here'. Fix: either remove 'private' to make it package-private (default), or make it 'public'. If Config is an INNER class (declared inside another class), then 'private class Config' is perfectly valid — private inner classes are fully supported and commonly used to hide helper classes.

Line A compiles and prints 10. Line B causes a COMPILE ERROR. This is the protected cross-package access rule: A subclass (Child) in a different package (com.b) CAN access a parent's protected member through its OWN reference (Line A — 'value' implicitly means 'this.value'). However, it CANNOT access the protected member through a Parent-type reference (Line B — 'p.value') from a different package. The inheritance privilege only applies to the subclass's own inherited copy, not to arbitrary parent-type objects.

Fixed version: public class Team { private String teamName; private List<String> members = new ArrayList<>(); public Team(String teamName) { if (teamName == null || teamName.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); this.teamName = teamName; } public String getTeamName() { return teamName; } public void addMember(String member) { if (member != null && !member.isBlank()) members.add(member); } public void removeMember(String member) { members.remove(member); } public List<String> getMembers() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(members); } public int getMemberCount() { return members.size(); } } — Fields are private, collection exposed as unmodifiable, business methods control all mutations.

start() override: COMPILE ERROR. Truck tries to reduce 'start()' from public (Vehicle) to protected (Truck). This narrows access — illegal in Java. Override rule: visibility can only stay the same or increase. Fix: 'public void start()' in Truck. stop() override: VALID. Truck widens 'stop()' from protected (Vehicle) to public (Truck). Widening is always allowed. This is correct overriding. Summary: protected → public ✅ (widening), public → protected ❌ (narrowing — compile error).

Output: 'Animal sound'. This demonstrates that private methods are NOT polymorphic. Dog.sound() is NOT an override of Animal.sound() — it is a completely new, unrelated method. Animal.makeSound() calls 'sound()' which resolves to Animal's own private sound() at compile time (static binding). Even though 'a' holds a Dog object at runtime, the private method call in Animal.makeSound() is bound to Animal.sound() — Dog's sound() is invisible to Animal. This is a classic interview trap. If sound() were public/protected in Animal, Dog.sound() would be a proper override and 'Woof' would print.

items.q: 7. Design a class using all four access modifiers appropriately for a Library system book checkout.
items.a: public class LibraryBook { private final String isbn; private final String title; private boolean checkedOut; private String borrowerName; private int checkoutCount; protected static final int MAX_RENEWAL_DAYS = 14; public LibraryBook(String isbn, String title) { this.isbn = isbn; this.title = title; this.checkedOut = false; this.checkoutCount = 0; } public String getIsbn() { return isbn; } public String getTitle() { return title; } public boolean isAvailable() { return !checkedOut; } public void checkOut(String borrower) { if (checkedOut) throw new IllegalStateException("Already checked out"); this.checkedOut = true; this.borrowerName = borrower; this.checkoutCount++; } public void returnBook() { if (!checkedOut) throw new IllegalStateException("Not checked out"); this.checkedOut = false; this.borrowerName = null; } int getCheckoutCount() { return checkoutCount; } // default — package-level reporting private boolean isPopular() { return checkoutCount > 50; } } — private: isbn, title, checkedOut, isPopular(). default: getCheckoutCount() for package reporting. protected: MAX_RENEWAL_DAYS for subclass LibraryEBook. public: checkout API.

Compile error: Document.print() reduces the interface method's implicit public access to default (package-private). Interface abstract methods are implicitly public. When a class implements an interface method, it must use the same or wider access — which means it MUST be public. The error is: 'print() in Document cannot implement print() in Printable; attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public'. Fix: 'public void print() { System.out.println("Printing document"); }'. This is a very common mistake for developers coming from languages with different interface rules.

sections.title: Conclusion — Access Modifiers: The Gatekeepers of Java OOP

blocks.text: Access modifiers are not just a syntactic detail — they are the architectural foundation of well-designed Java code. They enforce encapsulation, define public contracts, protect internal invariants, and make codebases maintainable as they grow. Every field, method, and class you write deserves a deliberate access modifier choice — not a default assumption.

The golden rule professionals follow: start with the most restrictive modifier and only promote when genuinely necessary. Begin every field as private. Begin every helper method as private. Promote to default when package-level sharing is needed. Promote to protected only for deliberate inheritance contracts. Promote to public only for the intentional external API. This discipline — called the Principle of Least Privilege — is what separates maintainable enterprise Java from fragile, tightly-coupled code.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Access Modifiers

items.q: What are access modifiers in Java?
items.a: Access modifiers in Java are keywords that control the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, constructors, and fields. Java provides four access levels: public (accessible from anywhere), protected (same package and subclasses), default/package-private (same package only — no keyword), and private (same class only). They are the primary mechanism for implementing encapsulation — restricting internal details and exposing only what is necessary.

items.q: What is the difference between private, protected, and public in Java?
items.a: private: most restrictive — accessible only within the declaring class. protected: accessible within the same package AND in subclasses across packages. public: least restrictive — accessible from anywhere in the program. The rule: always use the most restrictive modifier that still allows your code to function. Start with private for fields and helpers, use public only for the intentional external API.

items.q: Can a class be private in Java?
items.a: A top-level class can only be public or default (package-private). Top-level private or protected classes cause a compile-time error. However, inner classes (declared inside another class) CAN be private, protected, public, or default. A private inner class is commonly used for helper classes or implementation details that should be hidden even from other classes in the same package.

items.q: What is default access modifier in Java?
items.a: The default access modifier (package-private) is applied when no modifier keyword is written. A member with default access is visible to all classes within the same package but completely hidden from classes in other packages — including subclasses in different packages. It has no keyword — writing 'default' as an access modifier is a compile error. It is suitable for package-internal implementation classes and utilities not meant to be part of the public API.

items.q: Can we override a private method in Java?
items.a: No. Private methods are not visible to subclasses, so they cannot be overridden. If a subclass declares a method with the same signature as a parent's private method, it creates an entirely new unrelated method in the subclass — not an override. Using @Override on such a method causes a compile error. Private methods are also not polymorphic — calls to private methods are resolved at compile time (static binding), not at runtime.
